    • Daniel Kahneman was one of the leading psychologists of our time.
    • Kahneman became well known in the field of behavioral economics.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 26.05.2025 in den Kategorien Uncategorized,Video Analysis mit 4 Kommentaren.

    Daniel Kahneman was one of the leading psychologists of our time. In his book Thinking, Fast and Slow, he presented extensive insights from his many years of research. This article explores how Kahneman’s findings, along with other insights from behavioral science, can be applied to (strategic and tactical) football analysis.

    Kahneman became well known in the field of behavioral economics. Together with his colleague Amos Tversky, he succeeded in combining insights from psychology with those of economics. In 2002, he became the first psychologist to be awarded the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences.

    It has been revealed that his research challenges the fundamental assumption that humans make rational decisions and that cognitive distortions are primarily driven by emotions. Instead, he argued that systematic thinking errors significantly influence our judgment and decision-making. These systematic errors, known as “biases,” occur in predictable ways under certain conditions.

    Industry observers note that kahneman’s work has been applied in fields such as medical diagnosis, the legal system, intelligence analysis, philosophy, statistics, and military strategy. It is therefore a logical step to apply his research to sports analysis, where strategic decisions also play a crucial role.

    Industry observers note that “I suppose that every author has in mind a situation in which readers of their work might benefit from reading it. I imagine the coffee machine at the office, where colleagues exchange opinions and gossip. My hope is to enrich the vocabulary people use when they talk about the judgments and decisions of others (…).” – Daniel Kahneman; Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    It has been revealed that A mere list of cognitive biases is not sufficient to recognize and avoid distortions in one’s own or others’ decisions. Only through a deeper understanding of their origins and mechanisms can the vocabulary around judgment and decision-making be enriched in Kahneman’s sense. Therefore, this article sheds light on the underlying processes and mechanisms of judgment and decision errors.

    It has been revealed that we begin by examining the scientifically established dual-process model. Following that, the mechanisms of WYSIATI, substitution, and priming will be explored in the context of football. In addition, the most relevant heuristics and cognitive biases will be applied to football analysis. Finally, we will address individual factors within analysis that contribute to the emergence of bias.

    This article is only the first part of a series, which will span at least three essays. The series will examine flawed judgments in football analysis and their causes within a scientific framework informed by behavioral research.

    One point should be made clear from the outset: bias (and noise) are present wherever decisions are made, and thus affect even expert judgments within their domain.

    This article is based on a German translation of Daniel Kahneman’s work. Accordingly, the quotes cited here may not exactly match the original English wording.

    To explain human thinking, Kahneman introduces two hypothetical agents: System 1 and System 2. This model provides a framework for understanding how thought processes work. System 1 is responsible for fast thinking, it operates automatically, intuitively, and with little effort. System 2, on the other hand, governs slow thinking, it works analytically, consciously, and requires effort.

    In a recent development, these two systems interact continuously whenever we are awake. System 1 runs constantly and automatically, while System 2 operates in an energy-saving mode, only stepping in occasionally. As a result, System 2 rarely takes control. Typically, System 2 adopts the impressions and intuitions generated by System 1 and accepts its intuitive responses.

    Industry observers note that the division of labor between the two systems is highly efficient. From an evolutionary perspective, this can be explained by the need to react quickly to threats while also engaging in deliberate, long-term planning. Thus, the automatic System 1 developed primarily for threat detection, while the energy-intensive System 2 evolved to support complex reasoning, though it is less frequently engaged in full.

    In a recent development, however, it is particularly System 1 that is susceptible to cognitive biases. Due to its energy efficiency, it is limited in logic and statistical reasoning. It often tends to substitute complex questions with simpler ones. System 2, in turn, tends to adopt these flawed outputs, as it does not always monitor or correct the conclusions generated by System 1.

    The following simple and intuitive thinking task illustrates the interplay between System 1 and System 2:.

    In a recent development, team A has 62% possession and wins a match 1-0. Team B has 38% possession and loses. Which team was more dominant?

    Of course, Team A was more dominant. At least, that’s the intuitive conclusion System 1 leads most people to. However, it neglects the fact that possession is not necessarily a reliable measure of dominance, and that match results are very imprecise indicators of performance. Despite lacking detailed data, System 1 assembles the question into a coherent picture. System 2 supports System 1’s incorrect solution, even though with minimal effort it could have reached the correct conclusion. However, System 2 is not consciously engaged.

    From this, it follows that people rely on mental shortcuts, so-called heuristics, to promptly solve complex problems. Heuristics are usually very helpful due to their efficiency but can sometimes lead to errors in judgment, known as biases. This is where the relevance for football analysis arises, as will be shown in the following section.

    “A heuristic is, technically defined, a simple procedure that helps us find adequate, though often imperfect, answers to difficult questions.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    First, I have linked a YouTube video that you should watch:.

    Sources indicate that even if you are already familiar with the video, its insights are remarkable. On the one hand, it can be concluded that focusing on one task can make us blind to other processes. To see and orient ourselves, we need a certain level of attention. However, the main insight of the video is that we cannot believe we have missed something so obvious. For those who did not see the gorilla, the player leaving the scene, or the curtain changing colors, it is unimaginable not to have noticed such obvious events.

    “We can be blind to the obvious, and we are also blind to our blindness.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Applied to our football analysis, this once again demonstrates how prone we are to errors. How can we direct our attention to all levels of football tactics when, at the slightest distraction, we don’t even see a gorilla? We are only just beginning to discover many additional dimensions of the game as reference points, alongside spatial considerations in positional play. It is not only individual situations that are overlooked due to lack of attention, but possibly entire dimensions and we may not even be aware of this.

    Recent findings suggest that we only realize our mistakes when we can no longer analyze a team with the tools we have. We follow our own subjective beliefs in analysis and overlook other logical conclusions that could have been drawn equally well from the existing data. This problem becomes particularly interesting when assessing tactical risk.

    Recent findings suggest that recall the earlier question where you were asked to judge a team’s dominance based on possession percentages and the match result. System 1 constructed the best story it could from high possession and a win. What was not done, however, was likely questioning what is necessary to authentically assess a team’s dominance. We are blind to what we do not pay attention to.

    Hasty conclusions based on limited data form the basis of many heuristics. Kahneman refers to these conclusions as “What You See Is All There Is” (WYSIATI).

    “It is easier to fit everything you know into a coherent pattern when you know very little.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Recent findings suggest that this central mechanism explains why consistency of information, rather than its completeness, is what primarily shapes our beliefs. Unfortunately, we also interpret information accordingly through our coherence-seeking System 1. Kahneman explains that System 1 is completely insensitive to the quality and quantity of information from which impressions and intuitions arise. System 1 looks for coherent information, while a lazy System 2 fails to check it.

    In a recent development, “They did not want more information that might spoil their story. WYSIATI.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    To start, I have prepared a question that should first be answered:.

    How successful will Relationism be compared to Positionism in the next ten years in the top 5 leagues?

    The answer will follow at the end of this section….

    Recent findings suggest that to interpret actions and processes, a complex, multidimensional understanding of the game is necessary. In analysis, we face difficult questions that can be answered on multiple levels. Often, there is not just one correct analysis, but several possibilities which together create an accurate picture.

    According to recent reports, “I know that I know nothing.” (cf. Plato, Apology 22d: “For I was conscious that I knew practically nothing…” ).

    Through reflection and the constant questioning of our observations and conclusions, we come closer to the goal of better understanding the game. The ability to accept that there are always latest perspectives and interpretations fosters a deeper, more nuanced understanding. Unfortunately, when faced with complex matters, humans intuitively tend to fall into different patterns of thinking.

    In a recent development, kahneman explains that even with complex questions, we rarely seem overwhelmed. We are able to provide answers to questions we do not fully understand. But why is that?

    Sources indicate that heuristics, as explained above, can be defined as mental shortcuts. Unfortunately, complex questions must also be answered in an energy-efficient way. Thus, we tend to substitute complex questions with simpler ones. This concept underlying many heuristics is called substitution. Often, we do not even notice that we have replaced a difficult question. However, we then use the answer to the simpler question to respond to the complex one. System 1 strives for the simplest possible answer to a question, while System 2, due to its inertia, does not verify the answer.

    “You are not overwhelmed, you don’t have to exert much effort, and you may not even notice that you have not answered the question that was asked of you.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    In a recent development, the concept of substitution is particularly pronounced when emotions are involved in the actual target question. Emotional attitudes amplify the effect. In the case of the so-called affect heuristic (judgments based on emotions), the interaction between System 1 and System 2 is especially prone to disruption. In the context of emotions and attitudes, System 2 does not act as a self-critic but rather as an advocate for the answer proposed by System 1. It looks for arguments that support its own beliefs.

    Recent findings suggest that let us return to the question posed at the beginning of this section. You most likely found an answer to how successful Relationismus will be in the future. However, instead of systematically thinking through the target question, an answer intuitively came to you that corresponds to your beliefs. The heuristic question you unconsciously answered might have been: How much do I like Guardiola’s Positionismus?

    Sources indicate that instead of searching for counterarguments against the intuitive answer, you subsequently searched for arguments that support your beliefs. To make a reliable future prediction, it would actually be necessary to free oneself from prejudices and break down the problem into its components, systematically questioning in which situations relational play is superior to positional play and in which situations the opposite is true. After all, the two philosophies can also be combined.

    It can be concluded that substitution, together with WYSIATI, forms two of the most important mechanisms in the interplay of System 1 and System 2 underlying many systematic cognitive errors. The following section will introduce another mechanism: priming.

    Priming is a fundamental mechanism that explains how we process information when thinking. Our memory plays a central role in this, more precisely, the way it connects information. This principle is called association.

    Kahneman uses a metaphor to explain association: “Like ripples on the surface of a pond, activation spreads through a small part of the vast network of associated representations.” Even a single stimulus can be enough to unconsciously activate adjacent concepts or memories.

    It has been revealed that A priming effect occurs when a specific stimulus, a word, an image, a situation, etc. unconsciously activates certain content in memory. This automatic chain of activation influences how we think, feel, or act without us noticing. The brain essentially lays down mental pathways in the associative network, thereby facilitating the unconscious retrieval of information.

    To illustrate, here is a simple example: “If you have recently seen or heard the word eat, you will be temporarily more likely to complete the word fragment so_p as soup rather than soap. The opposite would happen if you had just seen the word wash.”– Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Industry observers note that priming is already being used effectively in football contexts. For example, tactical training that includes video analysis and corresponding training formats represents a form of priming. By showing (tactical) videos during team meetings or recreating game-like patterns in training sessions, players can recognize familiar situations during matches, allowing them to react more swiftly and effectively. Training decision-making under pressure and developing speed of action can therefore be linked to the priming effect.

    Another well-known example of this effect is the “Florida effect.” For those interested in reading more, I’ve linked the original 1996 study by John A. Bargh, Mark Chen, and Lara Burrows.

    Priming also plays a role in many other areas of football. It can be deliberately used to create positive outcomes, but it can also have unintended negative effects. Depending on the context, different types of priming are distinguished, such as semantic priming, affective priming, goal priming, and many more. In football, priming is also used, for example, in injury prevention and rehabilitation.

    Priming can also be used for the cognitive preparation of a match. In the so-called “Moments of Excellence,” players consciously recall their best past performances immediately before a game. Particularly interesting is the application of “success priming” by the coach, through the use of specific words or phrases in the pre-match talk. Attached is a 2006 study by Stajkovic, Locke, and Blair on this topic, specifically on the unconscious performance enhancement through goal activation.

    Sources indicate that analysts, too, are subject to unconscious priming. A glance at the final score before conducting an analysis primes their expectations and subtly shifts the approach toward explaining the outcome, even though the final score, due to its inaccuracy as a performance indicator, says little about a team’s actual dominance.

    Sources indicate that given the scope of the subject, an entire article could likely be written solely on the use of priming in football. In this article, however, the foundations of priming are used to understand it as one of the mechanisms underlying cognitive biases that affect football analysis.

    “They were primed to find flaws, and that is exactly what they found.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Industry observers note that note: An earlier version mentioned the so-called “Florida Effect.” This belongs to a group of priming phenomena that, in the context of the replication crisis, have been only weakly or not at all confirmed. Those interested in learning more can find further information in the comment section. Many thanks to “AG” for the attentive feedback!

    It has been revealed that at the beginning of the introduction, I explained that distortions in our thinking and decision-making occur in predictable ways under certain conditions. By now, you should have developed a basic understanding of how our thinking is governed by the interaction between System 1 and System 2, how intuitive judgments arise in the process of analysis, and how mechanisms such as WYSIATI, substitution, and priming can specifically contribute to systematic biases in football analysis.

    So far, around 200 cognitive biases have been identified. However, unlike many other articles that present a long list of biases with only brief descriptions, I deliberately refrain from doing so here. In my view, a simple enumeration does little to help recognize or avoid these distortions in practice. Instead, I focus on a small number of key biases that are particularly relevant to football analysis. Part 2 of this series will examine additional biases in the context of overconfidence.

    It has been revealed that “Coherence means that you’re going to adopt one interpretation in general. Ambiguity tends to be suppressed. This is part of the mechanism that you have here that ideas activate other ideas and the more coherent they are, the more likely they are to activate to each other. Other things that don’t fit fall by the wayside. We’re enforcing coherent interpretation. We see the world as much more coherent than it is.” – Daniel Kahneman, Edge.

    What Kahneman describes here is the phenomenon called associative coherence. The processing of subjectively fitting information is facilitated by associative memory, while the processing of mismatching information is hindered. System 1 thus generates a coherent pattern of activated ideas in associative memory.

    Recent findings suggest that this phenomenon inevitably leads to errors in analysis. We should be aware that our analysis alone will never capture the entirety of the subject being analyzed. The analysis is always an expression of the analyst’s beliefs and the ideas activated in their associative memory. Even though System 2 can counteract when activated, it is still influenced by System 1. The concept of associative coherence is therefore closely related to WYSIATI and priming.

    As part of the outcome of associative coherence, confirmation bias can be seen. It describes our tendency to want to confirm our existing beliefs.

    “The coherence of associative activation induces a confirmatory bias when people examine a hypothesis by increasing the accessibility of hypothesis-consistent information. For example, the intention to test the proposition that ‘Sam is friendly‘ preferentially activates evidence of Sam’s friendliness, whereas testing the proposition that ‘Sam is not friendly‘ preferentially evokes instances of hostile behavior.” – Associative Processes in Intuitive Judgement.

    Sources indicate that in analysis, we tend to seek out, select, and interpret information in a way that confirms our expectations. This, of course, applies to all areas of football analysis. Active countermeasures are necessary to avoid overlooking data that contradicts one’s own hypothesis.

    To simplify the illustration of anchoring, please answer the following two questions one after the other.

    Does Cristiano Ronaldo have more or less than 1,200 international matches for the senior national team?

    How many international matches for the senior national team has Cristiano Ronaldo played?

    It has been revealed that you have very likely come to the conclusion that Ronaldo has played fewer than 1,200 international matches. Nevertheless, this value probably influenced your estimate of the second question towards a number that is too high. Ronaldo has (as of March 2025) played 219 international matches.

    Industry observers note that judgments are often based on the first piece of information given, the anchor. This biases the estimate in its direction. Daniel Kahneman distinguishes two psychological mechanisms that explain this effect.

    Recent findings suggest that the anchoring effect is measured and demonstrated in most psychological studies using numerical estimates, for example by estimating prices or probabilities. However, such quantitative judgments are not directly present in video analysis in football. To nevertheless apply the anchoring effect to this context, a change of perspective is useful: Richards J. Heuer Jr., among others a former CIA analyst, investigated the influence of cognitive biases, including the anchoring effect, on qualitative judgment processes within the intelligence community. In his book Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, Heuer deliberately does not refer only to mere numerical estimates, but to all kinds of ongoing judgments or assessments that an analyst inherits from predecessors or gradually revises themselves. Empirical evidence for the effectiveness of anchoring effects in sports video analysis is still lacking, but an analogy via the intelligence community is plausible.

    As already described above, the match result provides the analyst with the first available piece of information, acting as a kind of anchor. A 4–0 or 2–1 score leads us to attribute tactical superiority to the winning team and to base our tactical assessments too strongly on the result.

    “We should, in any case, assume that every number presented to us has an anchoring effect on us (…).” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Another example of an anchoring effect in video analysis can be found when analyzing multiple matches of a team. The first game analyzed sets an initial assessment of the team’s tactical approach. As the analysis progresses, the analyst may need to revise their judgments but often fails to adjust sufficiently and remains primarily anchored to the initial assessment. This results in a biased analysis skewed toward the anchor game.

    „Even when analysts make their own initial judgment, and then attempt to revise this judgment on the basis of newly introduced information or further analysis, there is much evidence to suggest that they usually do not change the judgment enough.” – Psychology of Intelligence Analysis.

    It is not surprising that people look for reference points when faced with complex problems, the anchor provides exactly this orientation. Unfortunately, in certain cases, it distorts our decision-making. Mussweiler and Strack investigated in their study “Overcoming the Inevitable Anchoring Effect: Considering the Opposite Compensates for Selective Accessibility” how the anchoring effect can be mitigated. Simply being aware of the anchor and the effect is unfortunately not enough to avoid the bias. Instead, a strategy of deliberately thinking about the opposite proves effective in preventing it. Imagine, instead of a 4–0 victory, a 0–4 defeat, and consider how your analysis would look in that case.

    In a recent development, outcome Bias describes the tendency to judge performance based on the outcome. It is closely related to the principle of anchoring. The result serves as an anchor that shifts the judgment in its direction.

    Unlike the example mentioned above regarding bias from the match result, Outcome Bias can be applied to all types of results. This means that individual actions and sequences by players are evaluated based on their success or failure, regardless of the actual quality of execution.

    An example of this is a successful pressing sequence that leads to winning the ball. Because of the positive outcome, the pressing is overall rated as good. However, other relevant factors, such as intensity, timing, the opponent’s reaction, etc. are either not considered at all or only insufficiently taken into account.

    Sources indicate that if the same pressing sequence is executed again in a different game situation but fails to win the ball, the pressing is suddenly rated as poor, even though the execution was identical. This bias demonstrates how strongly the evaluation is influenced by the outcome rather than by the quality of the action itself. All actions in the game can be subject to Outcome Bias in analysis.

    It has been revealed that to prevent Outcome Bias, the evaluation criteria should be adjusted. Instead of judging a performance by its outcome, the process quality should be assessed. This increases the likelihood of future successful actions.

    The availability heuristic describes a cognitive shortcut in which people assess the frequency or likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind. In doing so, the original question: “How often does an event occur?” is replaced by a simpler one: “How easily can I recall relevant examples?”. This is a typical example of the substitution mechanism.

    More crucial for the availability of an action than the number of examples one can recall is how easily they come to mind, what is known as ease of retrieval. A paradoxical example illustrating the effect of the availability heuristic was demonstrated by Schwarz et al. in 1991: people are less convinced by a decision when asked to list as many arguments in favor of it as possible. This approach plays the two factors, number of arguments and ease of retrieval, against each other: the more arguments that must be generated, the harder they are to retrieve.

    Industry observers note that in the context of football analysis, this heuristic can lead to an overestimation of certain in-game actions or patterns, particularly during live matches. Striking, prominent, or emotional moments are more easily remembered and therefore disproportionately influence our overall evaluation of the game, regardless of how frequent or relevant they actually were. The availability heuristic has a particularly strong impact on our perception of risk (explored in Part 2).

    The game scenes most readily accessible to the analyst are also heavily influenced by their subjective experiences. A wide range of impressions, such as those from previous roles, past matches, or preferred playing philosophies, shape which factors and thus which moments are emphasized in the analysis. A strong bias toward particular strategies, such as overloads in possession, can distort the analysis by neglecting other decisive elements like timing. This simply stems from the complexity and diversity inherent to football. In this way, personal experience encourages subjective conclusions through the combination of the availability heuristic and WYSIATI.

    According to recent reports, the representativeness heuristic describes judgments about probability based on how representative something appears to be. Representativeness here refers to stereotypes and perceived similarity. When asked about probability, people often engage in substitution, evaluating plausibility instead of actual likelihood. Kahneman illustrates this with the following example:.

    “You see a person reading The Upcoming York Times on the New York subway. Which of the following is a better bet about the reading stranger?

    She does not have a college degree.”.

    While the more plausible story might lead you to bet on the PhD, you should consider the base rates. Given that far more people without a college degree ride the New York subway than people with doctorates, the statistically sounder bet would be on the person not having a college degree. This example highlights the tension between base rate information and representativeness.

    “The representativeness heuristic is misleading when it causes people to ignore base rate information that points in a different direction.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    Sources indicate that kahneman accordingly advises questioning the informativeness of data and anchoring probability judgments to plausible base rates. To further illustrate the relevance of this concept in a football context, consider the following recent example:.

    At the beginning of the 2024/25 season, Bayern Munich employed an aggressive, man-marking high press. This tactical approach faced heavy criticism, primarily due to the potential for conceding counterattack goals. Despite the fact that several clubs, such as Atalanta Bergamo, had already been successfully using man-marking in high pressing for years on the international stage, the approach was viewed as atypical in Germany. Since the 1990s, man-marking had largely been replaced in the Bundesliga by zonal marking or hybrid forms. The evaluation of Bayern’s pressing was guided by historical prototypes of man-marking, particularly those involving a libero and, thus, a structural numerical inferiority. Although the man-marking was implemented in a completely different tactical fashion, the comparison seemed plausible due to the similarity and influenced judgments about its success.

    In reality, the base rates painted a different picture: Bayern dominated their early Bundesliga matches, prevented opponents from gaining a foothold, and significantly limited their scoring opportunities. Statistically, the approach was highly successful: in their first 11 matches, 7 opponents failed to exceed an xG value of 0.5. The previous season’s champions, Leverkusen, only managed an xG of 0.17 and just 27% possession.

    Recent findings suggest that nonetheless, the assessment of Bayern’s man-marking pressing was distorted by the representativeness heuristic: instead of evaluating the actual likelihood of success based on objective data, the plausibility of an outdated playing style was used as the basis of judgment. This illustrates how stereotypical mental models can lead to misjudgments and how crucial it is to critically examine information in football analysis.

    For the sake of completeness, it should be mentioned that individual statistics (base rates in football) are not necessarily meaningful on their own. However, a combination of multiple statistics and data points can produce a more reliable picture to guide analysis. While xG values (as a combination of several data inputs) are still prone to error and need to be contextualized, they can nonetheless provide valuable insights into a team’s actual performance over time.

    The conjunction fallacy is one of the cognitive errors that arise from the representativeness heuristic. It describes the tendency of people to judge the combination of two events as more likely than one of the events alone, even when directly compared. The prerequisite is that the combination creates a more coherent and plausible story than the single event. One of the most controversial and well-known examples is the “Linda problem” by Kahneman and Tversky:.

    “Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student, she was deeply concerned with complications of discrimination and social justice, and also participated in anti-nuclear demonstrations.

    Which of the following is more probable?

    Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement.”.

    Despite the intuitive plausibility that Linda’s characteristics align more closely with the feminist movement, the first option is statistically more probable. After all, the conjunction of two events (“Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement”) is always less likely than one of the events alone (“Linda is a bank teller”).

    Industry observers note that „The most representative outcomes combine with the personality description to yield the most coherent stories. The most coherent stories are not necessarily the most probable, but they are plausible, and the concepts of coherence, plausibility, and probability are easily confused by the unwary.“ – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    It has been revealed that the “less-is-more pattern” by Christopher Hsee ties into this problem. For those who want to read more, I’ve linked the relevant study here. It states that the probability of the broader event (e.g., Linda is a bank teller) must be higher than that of the event that is included within it (e.g., Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement). However, the more plausible event (less comprehensive) is judged to be more probable than the less plausible, more comprehensive one. This creates the “less-is-more” pattern. As a result, the probability estimate for the more detailed scenario is higher, even though this contradicts logical reasoning.

    “This is the trap for forecasters and their clients: the more detailed the scenarios, the more convincing they are, but the less probable they become.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow.

    In the context of opponent team analysis for an upcoming match, the analyst must be aware that they are the forecaster, making probability estimates about the opponent’s future style of play. Thus, they should assess the likelihood of events, not merely their plausibility.

    In a recent development, applying Hsee’s “less-is-more principle” to this context means that detailed, plausible match scenarios may sound impressive, but are statistically less reliable for prediction than broader descriptions. Each additional assumption in a forecast multiplies individual probabilities and thereby reduces the overall likelihood of an accurate prediction.

    Sources indicate that however, this is not a call for a lack of detail in opponent analysis. On the contrary, the more detailed, precise, and comprehensive the analysis, the better the ability to derive general playing principles, patterns, and behaviors of the opponent. Therefore, the analyst should aim to analyze the opponent as holistically as possible before making generalized statements that increase the predictive probability.

    While in Part 2 I will address structural conditions in football that affect the intuition of analyst and coach experts, in this section I will focus on the individual conditions of different types of analysis. Even though I speak here about football analysis in general, it is vital to clarify that there are various forms of analysis in football (see table). Different types of analysis also have different individual susceptibilities to cognitive biases.

    In a recent development, certain biases are additionally triggered by specific types of analysis. Prediction, for example, is particularly affected by the representativeness heuristic, since it involves assessing probabilities. Team analysis over multiple games increases susceptibility to the anchoring heuristic, and post-match analysis is prone to hindsight bias, the tendency to overestimate the predictability of an event after it has occurred.

    Recent findings suggest that similarly, focusing on a single level of analysis increases vulnerability to WYSIATI. You should now be familiar with the cognitive errors mentioned here, so they should not come as a surprise. One factor not yet addressed in this article, which demonstrably increases susceptibility to all biases, is time pressure. Time pressure plays a significant role especially during live analysis, though not exclusively.

    Recent findings suggest that time pressure forces analysts to make quicker decisions. Research reveals that under such conditions, people rely more heavily on heuristics, increasing the likelihood of errors. Among other studies, Finucane et al. (2000) examined the influence of the affect heuristic on the evaluation of benefits and risks, demonstrating that time pressure amplifies this effect.

    Analysts therefore have to rely more on their intuition during live analysis. This brings me to Part 2, where I will identify conditions that increase experts’ susceptibility to intuitive errors.

    By now, it should be clear why we delve so deeply into the mechanisms of heuristics. Without a fundamental understanding of how they work, heuristics and cognitive biases are difficult to recognize.

    Many behavioral psychology insights can be profitably applied in sports analysis. This includes not only heuristics and cognitive biases but can also be extended to other areas of football analysis. However, to cover these application areas sufficiently, there will be a Part 2, Part 3, and, if necessary, a Part 4.

    In Part 2, I will address the topic of overconfidence. Among other things, it will examine the susceptibility of expert intuition as well as risk strategies and risk assessments in football. Strategies for avoiding biases in football analysis will also be presented.

    Recent findings suggest that part 3 (and possibly Part 4) will focus on “noise” in football analysis. Unlike bias, noise does not describe the distortion of judgments in a particular direction but the unconscious variability of multiple judgments under identical decision conditions.

Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Philadelphia 76ers are off to a fantastic start to the 2026-27 season at 12-3, good for first in the Eastern Conference, and perhaps most encouraging for the Sixers is that they're winning without looking like a team playing at its absolute peak.

    According to recent reports, after a huge offseason adding LeBron James and Jaylen Brown, the Sixers still look like a team figuring out how best to work together, but when it comes time in the fourth quarter to find a way to win, they manage to get the job done. Tyrese Maxey is leading the way with Brown quickly finding his rhythm, but James and Joel Embiid in particular still seem to be feeling it out early in the season.

    James, who has never averaged less than 20.9 points per game in his previous 23 seasons, is averaging just 15.1 points per game and his 44.3/22.5/71.7 shooting splits are all career lows or close to it. As James figures things out, ESPN reported that a Sixers source claimed James "asked coaches to be patient with him as he expects to find his rhythm and get his conditioning in line by December as he ramps up.".

    That report hit social media and caught James' attention, with the 41-year-old star denying ever saying that.

    It has been revealed that ESPN didn't report a direct quote from James, and it's very possible the Sixers source offered an anecdote that paraphrased James and used the word patience when James never did. That then ended up on a social media graphic and prompted James to shoot it down.

    Industry observers note that what's fascinating here is it's not a scathing report or even anything particularly juicy. James is struggling with his shot early in the year and seems to be figuring out exactly where he fits in the offense alongside Maxey, Brown and Embiid as a scorer. He's still doing plenty of things well -- including leading the team with 6.9 assists per game and just took over third all-time in assists in NBA history -- and the Sixers are still winning even with James ice cold with his jumper, which history suggests will turn around at some point.

    Patience would be prudent from the Sixers with James, whether he wants to use that word or not, and it seems like a matter of when, not if, he gets shots to start falling and the Philly offense becomes even more dynamic.

    10 most interesting MLB non-tender decisions, including a Red Sox staple and a former Rookie of the Year

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 20, is an important date on MLB's offseason calendar.
    • Sources indicate that dozens of players are non-tendered every offseason when teams determine their production no longer warrants the salary.
    • It has been revealed that with that in mind, here are the 10 most interesting non-tender decisions ahead of Friday's deadline, using the arbitration salary projections at the indispensable MLB Trade Rumors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This Friday, Nov. 20, is an important date on MLB's offseason calendar. It is the deadline for teams to offer 2027 contracts to their arbitration-eligible and pre-arbitration players. The player does not have to sign by Friday's 5 p.m. ET deadline, but he must be offered a contract. If he's not, the player is considered non-tendered and immediately becomes a free agent.

    Sources indicate that dozens of players are non-tendered every offseason when teams determine their production no longer warrants the salary. Adolis García, Nathaniel Lowe, Alek Manoah, and Christopher Morel were among the notable non-tenders last offseason. Go back a few years and major names like Cody Bellinger and Kyle Schwarber were non-tendered.

    It has been revealed that with that in mind, here are the 10 most interesting non-tender decisions ahead of Friday's deadline, using the arbitration salary projections at the indispensable MLB Trade Rumors. You can be sure these teams will scour the trade market for these players and try to get something back before making the non-tender official.

    Projected salary: $11.1 million (team control through 2028).

    Duran was a non-tender candidate even before the Jake Bauers signing pushed him out of the everyday lineup. There is no such thing as too many good players, but the Red Sox now have two first basemen (Bauers and Willson Contreras) and four outfielders (Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela). Mickey Gasper and Masataka Yoshida are still around too. That's eight players for five lineup spots (first base, DH, three outfield spots). On any given day, three of those guys will be on the bench. Duran, who got MVP votes in 2024, had a 20-20 season in 2026, but it came with a ballooning strikeout rate and a .266 on-base percentage. He has been on the trade block for close to two years now and the writing is on the wall. If the Red Sox are unable to trade Duran this week, there's a real chance he'll get non-tendered Friday given his hefty salary projection.

    Projected salary: $7.7 million (team control through 2028).

    Former No. 1 overall draft picks have been non-tendered in the past (Tim Beckham most recently), just not by the team that drafted them. Non-tendering Torkelson would be a tough look for the Tigers even though he has not developed into the impact hitter he was projected to be coming out of Arizona State. Simply put, the salary is beginning to outweigh the production. Torkelson, 27, is a 25-30 homer bat with one of the league's highest strikeout rates, middling on-base percentages, and no secondary value (defense, baserunning, etc.). That remarked, the Tigers do not have an obvious replacement first baseman ready to step in (Colt Keith was the backup in 2026). That, plus the fact that Torkelson has No. 1 pick pedigree, could keep him in Detroit another year.

    Projected salary: $2.3 million (team control through 2029).

    The American League Rookie of the Year in 2024, Gil has battled injuries and ineffectiveness in the two seasons since. The swing-and-miss rate on his fastball went from an elite 28.5% in 2024 to a below-average 18.8% in 2025 and 17.4% in 2026. Gil, 28, spent time in Triple-A this past season and the Yankees moved him into the bullpen late in the year, where the results were so-so. The salary projection is a pittance, particularly for a team with Fresh York's payroll, though Gil is now out of minor-league options (he must pass through waivers to go to Triple-A) and doesn't have an obvious role. Because he is a pitcher and breathing, and also has a major award win in the not-too-distant past, the Yankees might be able to find a trade partner this week. If not, Gil is a definite non-tender candidate.

    Projected salary: $7.6 million (team control through 2028).

    A fan favorite and an All-Star this past season, Clement crashed hard in the second half, and the fact of the matter is he has a .295 on-base percentage in his three full seasons with the Blue Jays. Also, the soon-to-be 31-year-old's defensive numbers tumbled this year. Clement's contact skills are elite and he's a versatile, high-energy player. As a utility guy, he's an ace. As an everyday player, he's stretched. Clement's projected salary is hefty for a utility player, particularly one with limited offensive upside who no longer reliably catches the baseball. My guess is the Blue Jays will keep him and live with the salary, but it's not an obvious decision.

    Projected salary: $5.1 million (team control through 2028).

    In a recent development, similar to Torkelson, non-tendering a former No. 1 overall pick would be a tough look for the Twins, but a clean break might be best for all involved at this point. Lewis, 27, has trended down since his boffo second half in 2023, enough that he was sent to Triple-A for a spell this summer. He's also moved down the defensive spectrum from third base to first base. It's not due to a lack of effort; Lewis is a major tinkerer who has tried all sorts of swing adjustments. It just hasn't come together. A fresh start elsewhere, away from the spotlight of former No. 1 pick and face of the franchise, might be best for him. The budget-conscious Twins could then reallocate the projected $5.1 million elsewhere on the roster. Right now, they can't count on Lewis to hit or have a meaningful impact defensively.

    Projected salary: $3.4 million (team control through 2028).

    Industry observers note that in 2023, Gorman slugged 27 home runs and looked like one of baseball's top young power hitters. In the three seasons since, he has not come close to repeating that success. The hope was that moving him to third base, his natural position, would unlock Gorman's offense following the Nolan Arenado trade. That didn't happen, and Gorman spent a major chunk of the summer in Triple-A, where he continued to have a hard time making contact. Now 26, Gorman has a minor-league option remaining and can go to Triple-A again in 2027, but the signs are not subtle. The Cardinals are reportedly seeking a stopgap third baseman until top prospect Jesús Báez is ready, which would likely not be the case if they had any belief in Gorman. That projected $3.4 million salary is a high price for a reclamation project ticketed for the minors.

    Projected salary: $6.9 million (team control through 2028).

    Right-handed power is in short supply throughout baseball and Burger, 31 in April, has hit at least 28 home runs in three of the last four years. He is a one-tool player, though. The home runs come with low batting averages, low on-base percentages, higher-than-average strikeout rates, and little to no defensive or baserunning value. Rangers president of baseball operations Chris Young mentioned his team lacked "grit and toughness," whatever that means, and indicated he wants more hitters who grind out at-bats. That's not Burger, who can hit the ball a mile but is not known for making life tough on pitchers. The $6.9 million projection could be deemed too pricey for a player with such a limited skill set.

    Projected salary: $6.6 million (team control through 2027).

    Doval went from the Yankees to the Pirates at the trade deadline, then from the Pirates to the Giants on waivers in September. He's a former All-Star who led the National League in saves in 2023, two things that have boosted his arbitration salaries. Since 2023, Doval has been a middle reliever who was on the outside of the Circle of Trust™ more often than not. The 29-year-old righty still throws very hard. There's nothing wrong with his arm. It's hard to believe he gets hit as hard as he does sometimes. Doval earned $6.1 million in 2026 and a player cannot have a salary cut by more than 20% during his team control years. That would set Doval's minimum 2027 salary at $4.88 million. I wonder if the Giants would offer him a pay cut, say $5.5M or so, and tell him it's either that or a non-tender. That happens a few times a year around the league.

    Projected salary: $6.5 million (team control through 2027).

    A fan favorite in San Diego -- "Ho-ly Sheets!" chants are commonplace during his at-bats at Petco Park -- Sheets has fallen by the wayside a bit with the Padres, so much so that he started just one of their six postseason games this year. The 30-year-old is a platoon player who is good against righties more than great and is a defensive liability at both first base and left field. Realistically, Sheets is a platoon DH, and teams rarely pay well for that role unless they're confident they will get substantial offensive numbers. In the grand scheme of things, the projected $6.5 million isn't much. It is top-of-the-market dollars for this skill set, however.

    Projected salary: $1.4 million (team control through 2029).

    Two years ago, Blanco threw a no-hitter in his eighth career start. This year, he was so far out of the picture that he pitched once in Houston's last 12 games (two innings at the end of a 13-2 blowout), and the Astros opted to start Peter Lambert on two days' rest with a postseason spot on the line in Game 162. Blanco, who is older than you may realize (he turned 33 in August), returned from Tommy John surgery this summer and had a rough go of it. The pitching-needy Astros could send him to Triple-A next season, as he has a minor-league option remaining, but his stuff was diminished after surgery, and again, they didn't trust him late in the year. You would be surprised at how many cheap pitchers get non-tendered every year. Blanco could join them this week.

    Both of these teams are in desperation mode when it comes to needing victories for the postseason. The Ravens lost at home Monday night to the previously winless Chargers and now have to head out on the road on a short week. That's tough. The Panthers played better defense last week against the Saints, which will help them here. Carolina wins it late, but it's close.

    The Chargers won for the first time on Monday night, beating the Ravens on the road. They actually demonstrated some offensive life in that game. The Jets have defensive concerns, which the Chargers can take advantage of here. Quarterback Geno Smith is banged up for the Jets, which could mean rookie Cade Klubnik makes his first NFL start. Look for the Chargers to take advantage if that is the case as they get to 2-8 behind another solid showing by the offense.

    Fernando Mendoza will be making his first road start, which can be tough for a rookie. But it's also against a really good defense coming off a bye in a tough place to play. That's a real challenge. Look for the Broncos to get after him in this one. The Raiders' defense isn't playing well, so maybe it's just what Bo Nix needs. Broncos significant.

    This is a massive game for both teams. The Jaguars are 7-2 and playing as well as any team in the league. But they are playing consecutive road games against a Giants team pushing for a division title. This game will be decided by the Giants' defense against the Jaguars' offense. I think the Jaguars get the better of it. Look for them to run it well with Bhayshul Tuten.

    This is the best game of the week, featuring two of the NFC's best. The 49ers beat Dallas last week, while the Vikings beat the Packers in Kirk Cousins' first game back with the team after being traded by the Raiders. This will be about the 49ers offense vs. Brian Flores' defense. I think Kyle Shanahan will get the best of it as the 49ers keep rolling. Major day for Christian McCaffrey running it.

    It has been revealed that the Bengals are rolling on offense as Joe Burrow pushes toward the MVP. The Commanders have had problems against the pass, ranking 31st in the league, which has to have Burrow and the offense ready to go. Jayden Daniels won't keep up, but it's close. The Bengals keep rolling.

    Pick: Bengals 34, Commanders 30.

    Industry observers note that if the Texans are to have any chance of making the playoffs, they have to win this one. The Colts are pretty much done, but they beat Miami last week. Daniel Jones struggled in that one, but the Texans' defense has really struggled. Look for the Colts to hang around here, but the Texans will win it.

    #50480. NBA MVP Rankings: Luka Dončić, Victor Wembanyama in a two-horse race; Stephen Curry's absence speaks volumes

    NBA MVP Rankings: Luka Dončić, Victor Wembanyama in a two-horse race; Stephen Curry's absence speaks volumes

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We're nearly a month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and while some people say it's too early to start talking about MVP, we are not among those people.
    • Right now, it's a clear two-horse race: Luka Doncic or Victor Wembanyama?
    • In a recent development, the Luka Dončić we're watching right now isn't just the best offensive player in the world.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We're nearly a month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and while some people say it's too early to start talking about MVP, we are not among those people.

    Right now, it's a clear two-horse race: Luka Doncic or Victor Wembanyama? There is a real split on this. Here's where I stand as of Tuesday, Nov. 17.

    In a recent development, the Luka Dončić we're watching right now isn't just the best offensive player in the world. He might be the best in history. Nobody has ever put up anything close to the numbers he is charting at the moment: 39 points per game with seven assists, seven boards, nearly two steals and a positively scorching 66.0 TS%, the latter being a number even the great Stephen Curry has only bested twice in his career.

    It's early, sure. Dončić isn't likely to keep making 3s at this rate for an entire season, and indeed we've seen some slippage of late (35% over his last four, if you really want to split hairs), but his volume remains, with 4.5 makes a night over that stretch. Dončić remains on track to break Curry's single-season record of 402 3-pointers, and he's done more off-ball shooting than in the past.

    Throw in more transition production and a 53% midrange conversion rate, per Cleaning The Glass, and you're seeing a more diverse scorer, which is to say this isn't just a guy who has started off hot on his step-back 3s (though this is a major factor, too, of course), but a guy piercing defenses from more spots with different shots. If Dončić could actually be any harder to guard than he has been in the past, we're seeing it this season.

    He's also defending. His 23 steals rank sixth league-wide. Only two players have recovered more defensive loose balls than his eight. Only one has taken more charges than his four. With Dončić as the primary defender, shooters are converting just 36.7% of their shots against a 45.1 expected FG%; that minus-8.6 is the fourth-largest discrepancy among all players who've contested at least 150 shots.

    Industry observers note that most importantly, the Lakers are 12-2 and tied with the Spurs atop the Western Conference. The Lakers rank as the league's top offense with a rating that balloons to 129.2 points per 100 possessions (which would be an NBA record by a long shot) with Dončić on, and a net rating, as illustrated below, that falls off a cliff when he sits.

    In a recent development, look, if you have Wembanyama ahead of Dončić in the MVP race a month into the season, nobody is going to argue much with you. The oddsmakers slightly favor Wembanyama (+110 at FanDuel; Dončić is +140), who, as you'll see below, has what would qualify as a potentially unanimous case in most years. But this isn't most years. We got a dude averaging nearly 40 points for a No. 1 seed that nobody expected to be a No. 1 seed. Until one of those things changes, it's hard for me to go against Dončić.

    If you think Dončić's plus-35.5 on/off split (it's actually plus-32.2 without filtering for garbage time) is crazy, have a look at Wembanyama's number.

    Recent findings suggest that victor Wembanyama's impact this season has been another level. Spurs are +42.6 points per 100 possessions with Wemby on the court than off it, according to @cleantheglass. Small sample but other-worldly. Lakers star Luka Dončić is at +35.5 pts/100 poss.Both numbers are better… pic.twitter.com/0GJCFFmZ5K.

    Industry observers note that yes, you're reading that right. The Spurs, for all their supportive talent, fall by 42.6 points per 100 possessions when Wembanyama leaves the court (plus-29.2 on vs. minus-13.3 off), per Cleaning the Glass. By comparison, the best on/off split that Nikola Jokić has ever recorded is plus-24.8. Curry's best is plus-21.3. LeBron James' is plus-17.8. Go down that list and look at the most impactful on-off splits those guys have ever posted. Wembanyama is in another galaxy.

    And it's important to note that Wembanyama plays on a great team, as all these guys in the graphic have. The fact that there is still so much difference between when Wembanyama is on the court and when he isn't, even in a small sample, is honestly difficult to comprehend. San Antonio's three-guard lineup was supposed to be an experiment, but it's hard to know if Dylan Harper, De'Aaron Fox and Stephon Castle truly optimize one another or if Wembanyama is enough to make any lineup dominant in spite of traditional concerns (like none of those three being a true shooter).

    Sources indicate that wembanyama is the best defensive player on the planet by an immeasurable amount. Even the stats don't do it justice. He's on pace for north of 350 blocks, a number only four players (Elmore Smith, Mark Eaton, Manute Bol and Hakeem Olajuwon) have eclipsed since blocks became an official stat in 1973, and still it's just as much, if not more, about the shots he deters scorers from even attempting.

    It has been revealed that and why would they? Scorers are making just 33.6% of their shots when Wembanyama is the nearest defender, a 17% drop from their expected 50.4%. That also leads the league among all players who've defended at least 120 shots, and again, it fails to fully capture his defensive dominance.

    The fact that we've gotten this far without talking about Wembanyama's offense, as if it's a mere afterthought for a guy to be averaging 28.6 points and 11.6 rebounds in under 30 minutes a night. Wembanyama is figuring out his hot spots, prioritizing closer-to-the-basket positioning where he is a skyscraper among regular NBA buildings. He's taking two more paint shots per game than he did last season; 43% of his shots are coming from inside four feet, per Cleaning the Glass, up from 38% last season, and his 4.6 dunks per game (up from 2.7 last year) have him on pace to shatter Rudy Gobert's single-season record of 306.

    If I had to guess, Wembanyama's production is more sustainable than Dončić's. It's hard to imagine Dončić not hitting a rough patch from 3, and he's almost certainly not going to keep scoring 39 points per game. He'll be over 35 points per game when everything is noted and done because that's what the Lakers need from him, but there's a burnout factor while Wembanyama is kind of cruising to these numbers, and the defensive impact is as natural as breathing. My gut indicates Wembanyama will be a clearer MVP favorite by Christmas.

    Recent findings suggest that assuming Dončić and Wembanyama each get to the mandated 65 games, everyone else is playing for third place at the moment. Which is crazy given the seasons some of the following names are having.

    Industry observers note that one of two players averaging at least 22 points, nine rebounds and seven assists, and the only player to be leading his team in all three categories. The Rockets are 11-4 with the No. 2 offense and Sengun is the center of it all.

    According to recent reports, tatum is averaging his normal 26.5 points per game. The shooting efficiency still hasn't come around, but he is an absolute quarterback on this Celtics team. He draws the doubles, and his 35.1% assist rate, per CTG, is a career high by a mile. The Celtics, for my money, are the best team in the East.

    Cunningham is, once again, doing everything for the Pistons, who have been without Jalen Duren for all but the first four games and are still a top-three East seed. The 3-point shooting is down, but that's splitting hairs. This guy is shot-creating machine and, as forceful as he plays, he makes it look as smooth as anyone in the league.

    In a recent development, here come the Heat, who have won five straight games, with the last three wins coming over the Cavaliers, Pistons and Rockets. Antetokounmpo is averaging 28.3/12.5/5.2 with 1.3 blocks per game on 60% shooting. He's on fire from the midrange as the Heat are exploiting the soft spots in all the drop coverage they're facing.

    According to recent reports, gilgeous-Alexander has so much on his plate that it actually creates a clearer path to a third straight MVP if he can somehow lift Oklahoma City above all these injuries. He's trying. The Thunder are 9-5 and he's getting his 30.9 points per game, but his 58.7 true-shooting is down considerably, which makes sense as he has to force tougher shots now with fewer weapons around him.

    Recent findings suggest that curry's value can perhaps be felt most in his absence. The Warriors have lost three straight since he went out with a torn oblique, the last two by 59 points. The Warriors have outscored opponents by 13.5 points per 100 possessions with Curry on the floor this season and have been outscored by 8.3 points per 100 possessions without him. Along with Yaxel Lendeborg, who's being asked as a rookie to carry an impossibly heavy weight without Curry, Curry remains the only real lifeblood of a team that is still shockingly lifeless without him.

    2027 Baseball Hall of Fame ballot released: 8 things to know, including newcomers, trends and a prediction

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The ballot for the BBWAA portion of the 2027 Baseball Hall of Fame vote was revealed on Monday, featuring 13 holdovers and 14 newcomers.
    • The full ballot, in alphabetical order, is Bobby Abreu, Jake Arrieta, Jay Bruce, Mark Buehrle, Asdrúbal Cabrera, Starlin Castro, Wade Davis, Brett Gardner, Cole Hamels, Félix Hernández, Torii Hunter, Jon Lester, Andrew Miller, Dustin Pedroia, Andy Pettitte, Buster Posey, Alex Rodriguez, Francisco Rodríguez, Jimmy Rollins, Pablo Sandoval, Ervin Santana, Kyle Seager, Joakim Soria, Chase Utley, Omar Vizquel, David Wright and Ryan Zimmerman.
    • As a reminder, players must receive votes on at least 75% of the ballots cast to be inducted into the Hall of Fame with the 2027 class.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The ballot for the BBWAA portion of the 2027 Baseball Hall of Fame vote was revealed on Monday, featuring 13 holdovers and 14 newcomers.

    The full ballot, in alphabetical order, is Bobby Abreu, Jake Arrieta, Jay Bruce, Mark Buehrle, Asdrúbal Cabrera, Starlin Castro, Wade Davis, Brett Gardner, Cole Hamels, Félix Hernández, Torii Hunter, Jon Lester, Andrew Miller, Dustin Pedroia, Andy Pettitte, Buster Posey, Alex Rodriguez, Francisco Rodríguez, Jimmy Rollins, Pablo Sandoval, Ervin Santana, Kyle Seager, Joakim Soria, Chase Utley, Omar Vizquel, David Wright and Ryan Zimmerman. Newcomers to the ballot are in bold.

    As a reminder, players must receive votes on at least 75% of the ballots cast to be inducted into the Hall of Fame with the 2027 class. Those who get at least 5% of the vote can remain on the ballot the following year, and so on, for a maximum of 10 voting cycles. Players who are on the ballot for 10 years without getting 75% of the vote, in addition to players not getting 5% of the vote, fall off the ballot in ensuing years, though that doesn't mean the doors to the Hall are permanently shut.

    The results will be announced on Jan. 19, with the induction set for Cooperstown over the summer.

    Here's everything else you need to know about the Baseball Hall of Fame this offseason.

    Industry observers note that as alluded to earlier, there are two different votes each offseason. The BBWAA vote is for former players who have been retired from Major League Baseball for at least five years. It's the most common method in mainstream Hall of Fame ballot discussions. When you hear stuff like "first-ballot Hall of Famer," it means via the BBWAA vote.

    Sources indicate that players who don't make it via the BBWAA vote can get extra chances via committees. That's how, for example, Jeff Kent made it last year. Formerly called the Veterans Committee, the Hall of Fame now uses Era Committees, which are divided into two categories: contemporary baseball (1980 to present) and classic (prior to 1980). The contemporary ballot is then split into two, one for players and one for non-players like umpires, executives, pioneers and managers.

    Sure enough, this time around, it is a non-player Contemporary Baseball Committee, which looks at "managers, umpires and executives whose most significant career impact was realized since 1980.".

    We'll dive further into this group as we get closer to the Dec. 6 vote.

    Giants legend Buster Posey joins the ballot, and he's one of those cases where I don't think a bunch of people need to delve deeply into his numbers. More than statistics, sometimes we get "feel" guys, as in, you just know he's a Hall of Famer. Posey qualifies there, I would think, for 75% of the electorate. We'll obviously do a deeper dive in the coming weeks, but even without the longevity component (Posey only played in parts of 12 MLB seasons), I think he's in.

    As for the rest of the first-timers, the best case would be Jon Lester. Given the way a lot of similar starting pitchers have been treated in voting in recent years, my hunch is he'll be able to hang around on the ballot, but he has a major uphill battle in order to get in.

    It has been revealed that then you're looking at Brett Gardner, Ryan Zimmerman, Kyle Seager, the short peak of Jake Arrieta and relief work of Andrew Miller. Good players worth mentioning, of course, but they won't sniff the Hall and it seems likely all behind Posey and Lester are one-and-dones on this ballot, as they'll fall short of 5% of the vote.

    Sources indicate that this is the sixth year for Alex Rodriguez on the ballot, which means it's the sixth time that I point out that we don't really need much time to go over his case. His numbers say he's one of the 10 best position players of all time, but his ties to PEDs are keeping him out to this point.

    In a recent development, he did rise from 37.1% of the vote in 2025 to 40% last time, a fresh high-water mark. The progress is too modest to believe it's trending toward him getting in, but the number this year is certainly worth watching. If he somehow makes a leap to the 50% range, a deeper conversation might be in order.

    While some voters don't mind sending in blank ballots to prove some sort of nebulous point, most impose limits on themselves. Whether it's the actual rule of 10 or some voters saying they'll only vote, for example, for a maximum of three players on any given ballot, relatively weak ballots can leave openings for the best players to show huge gains. With Carlos Beltràn and Andruw Jones getting in last year and only one strong first-year candidate, perhaps Chase Utley can benefit.

    Utley is only in his fourth year on the ballot, but he's already made significant gains:.

    Recent findings suggest that he only needs to add 15.9 points after jumping nearly 20 last voting cycle. The situation is ripe for Utley to either get all the way in or get close enough to where he probably makes the Hall of Fame in 2028.

    Sources indicate that some of us are pushing to lower the Hall of Fame standard on modern starting pitchers, given the decreases in workload and how it affects their career numbers. We might be making some headway, but it's still tough sledding. Here are the holdover starting pitchers and their standing:.

    In a recent development, the bar for relievers to make the Hall of Fame is justly pretty high. We recently saw Billy Wagner make a late move and make it in his last try on the BBWAA ballot. Francisco Rodríguez has had four chances on the ballot and gotten between 7.8% and 11.8% of the vote thus far.

    K-Rod ranks sixth all time in saves and has good rate stats. He's worth tracking as it relates to three active relievers. Kenley Jansen is third in saves with a similar number of innings pitched to K-Rod. Craig Kimbrel is fifth and has more than 100 fewer innings pitched. Aroldis Chapman is ninth and in the ballpark of Kimbrel in workload to this point.

    If K-Rod continues to have trouble making headway toward induction, does that mean Kimbrel and Chapman will have trouble as well? What about Jansen?

    Who else is back on the ballot? A quick look:.

    In a recent development, posey is a lock. If the committee era chooses Bochy, Baker and/or Sabean, that would be some nice San Francisco flavor, too, right? I'll predict that committee ballot at a later date, though.

    I'll also say Utley's good roll here continues with a relatively weak ballot (at least when you factor in what the PED stain has done to some guys).

    On the player side, my 2027 Hall of Fame class prediction is Buster Posey and Chase Utley.

    This could be one of the best games of the season. You have a legitimate Super Bowl contender in the San Francisco 49ers facing off against a rejuvenated Minnesota Vikings team with Kirk Cousins at quarterback. This game will be played in Mexico City, and you should know that both teams have prepared for it differently.

    This stadium the 49ers and Vikings will play in on Sunday is over 7,000 feet above sea level. That led the 49ers to travel to the U.S. Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs this week, which is at a similar elevation of 6,621 feet, to prepare. The Vikings, on the other hand, built an altitude chamber so that players can get familiar with "thinner air" before Sunday. Otherwise, it looks like Minnesota is pulling a Los Angeles Rams and just showing up to a unique location the day before the game.

    In case you forgot, the 49ers dominated the Rams in Australia in the season opener, 27-7, and one reason why was because their travel looks were so much better. The 49ers have won and covered in four straight International games, and I think travel plans have a lot to do with that.

    The pick: 49ers -3.5Projected score: 49ers 26-20.

    Monday, 8:15 p.m. ET (ESPN, Stream: Fubo, try for free).

    Industry observers note that the Bengals are 0-2-1 in their last three games against the Washington Commanders, but I'll lay the points with the number under a full touchdown. The Bengals are 6-2 SU and 6-1-1 ATS in their last eight road games and have scored at least 30 points in three straight on the road.

    In a recent development, MVP favorite Joe Burrow is on pace for the highest completion percentage (74.7%) in a season in NFL history, and he also leads the league in passing yards per game (310.6), passing touchdowns (27) and passer rating (117.7). Burrow also has a dynamic duo that the Commanders simply aren't capable of containing. Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are on pace to become the first teammate duo to both record 1,500 receiving yards in a season.

    In a recent development, I don't think this game will be a blowout. Remember, the Bengals' defense struggled with Cam Ward and the Tennessee Titans, who took Cincy to overtime in Week 8. But I do think the Bengals can beat the Commanders by a touchdown.

    The pick: Bengals -6Projected score: Bengals 27-20.
